items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "polymer"?
options: A reaction in which two molecules are joined together with the removal of a molecule of water.
A large biological molecule such as a protein, polysaccharide or nucleic acid.
A giant molecule made from many similar repeating subunits (monomers) joined together.
A reaction in which a bond is broken by the addition of a molecule of water.
items.answer: A giant molecule made from many similar repeating subunits (monomers) joined together.
items.markingKey: Polymer: a giant molecule made from many similar repeating subunits (monomers) joined together.

items.stem: Explain why a sample must be neutralised after acid hydrolysis in the test for non-reducing sugar.
items.answer: Benedict's test only works in alkaline conditions; the acid would react with the Benedict's reagent, so it is neutralised with an alkali such as sodium hydrogencarbonate.
items.markingKey: Benedict's needs alkaline conditions [1]; neutralise acid [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why sucrose gives a negative result with Benedict's solution but a positive result after boiling with acid.
items.answer: In sucrose the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are used in the glycosidic bond, so it is non-reducing; acid hydrolyses the bond, releasing reducing monosaccharides.
items.markingKey: reducing groups involved in bond [1]; acid hydrolysis releases glucose / fructose [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana tested 3 unlabelled samples, P, Q, R. The results were: P: Benedict's brick-red; iodine orange-brown; biuret purple; emulsion white emulsion. Q: Benedict's blue; iodine blue-black; biuret purple; emulsion clear. R: Benedict's blue; iodine orange-brown; biuret blue; emulsion white emulsion. The samples were flour suspension, milk, vegetable oil. Identify each sample, giving a reason for each.
items.answer: P = milk; Q = flour suspension; R = vegetable oil.
items.markingKey: one mark per correct identification with reason linked to the test results [3]

items.stem: Arjun tested 4 unlabelled samples, P, Q, R, S. The results were: P: Benedict's blue; iodine blue-black; biuret purple; emulsion clear. Q: Benedict's blue; iodine orange-brown; biuret blue; emulsion white emulsion. R: Benedict's blue; iodine orange-brown; biuret purple; emulsion clear. S: Benedict's brick-red; iodine orange-brown; biuret purple; emulsion white emulsion. The samples were egg white, flour suspension, milk, vegetable oil. Identify each sample, giving a reason for each.
items.answer: P = flour suspension; Q = vegetable oil; R = egg white; S = milk.
items.markingKey: one mark per correct identification with reason linked to the test results [4]

items.stem: A food-science student in Nairobi is asked to find out which biological molecules are present in a new breakfast cereal. (a) Describe how the student would test for protein and state the positive result. (b) Suggest a suitable negative control for these tests.
items.answer: (a) Add biuret reagent (or NaOH then dilute CuSO₄) to a solution of the food; blue → purple. (b) Repeat each test with distilled water instead of the food sample to show the reagents alone do not give a positive result.
items.markingKey: (a) Add biuret reagent (or NaOH then dilute CuSO₄) to a solution of the food [1]; blue → purple [1] [2] (b) Repeat each test with distilled water instead of the food sample to show the reagents alone do not give a positive result [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a condensation reaction and a hydrolysis reaction, using maltose as an example.
items.answer: Condensation: two α-glucose join by a 1,4 glycosidic bond, releasing water, forming maltose. Hydrolysis: water is added to break the glycosidic bond, giving two α-glucose molecules.
items.markingKey: condensation removes water [1]; hydrolysis adds water [1]; example [1] [3]

items.stem: Mateo has a 10 % glucose solution and distilled water. Copy and complete a table to show the volumes needed to make 10 cm³ of each of these concentrations: 1 %, 5 %, 6 %. State the units in each column heading.
items.answer: 1 %: 1 cm³ stock + 9 cm³ water; 5 %: 5 cm³ stock + 5 cm³ water; 6 %: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water.
items.markingKey: V(stock) = C ÷ 10 × 10; one mark per correct row [3] ; headings with units, e.g. "volume of stock solution / cm³" [1] [4]

items.stem: A food-science student in Cape Town is asked to find out which biological molecules are present in a new breakfast cereal. (a) The Benedict's test is negative. Describe how the student could show whether a non-reducing sugar is present. (b) Describe how to test for lipid and explain why the food must not first be dissolved in water.
items.answer: (a) Boil with dilute HCl, cool, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, heat with Benedict's solution; brick-red precipitate = non-reducing sugar present. (b) Shake with ethanol, decant into water: white emulsion. Lipid is insoluble in water so it would not dissolve and be extracted.
items.markingKey: (a) any 3 from: Boil with dilute HCl; cool; neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate; heat with Benedict's solution; brick-red precipitate = non-reducing sugar present (1 mark each) [3] (b) Shake with ethanol [1]; decant into water: white emulsion [1]; Lipid is insoluble in water so it would not dissolve and be extracted [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "cellulose"?
options: A C–O–C bond formed by condensation between two monosaccharides.
A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or ribose, with the general formula (CH₂O)n.
A sugar made of two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, e.g. maltose, sucrose, lactose.
A polysaccharide of β-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds forming straight chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.
items.answer: A polysaccharide of β-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds forming straight chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.
items.markingKey: Cellulose: a polysaccharide of β-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds forming straight chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of starch makes it suitable as a storage molecule.
items.answer: Insoluble, so no osmotic effect and does not diffuse out of cells; compact (helical amylose); branched amylopectin gives many ends for rapid hydrolysis; made of α-glucose, easily hydrolysed to glucose for respiration.
items.markingKey: insoluble / no osmotic effect [1]; compact [1]; branches for rapid hydrolysis [1]; glucose released [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why glycogen is more suitable than starch as an energy store in animals.
items.answer: Glycogen is more highly branched, so has more ends for enzymes to act on, allowing glucose to be released more rapidly for the higher metabolic rate of animals.
items.markingKey: more branches [1]; more ends / faster hydrolysis [1]; animals more active / higher rate of respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: An unbranched chain of 12 α-glucose molecules is made by condensation. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. (a) State the number of glycosidic bonds. (b) Calculate the Mr of the chain.
An unbranched chain of 3 α-glucose molecules is made by condensation. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. (a) State the number of glycosidic bonds. (b) Calculate the Mr of the chain.

An unbranched chain of 8 α-glucose molecules is made by condensation. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. (a) State the number of glycosidic bonds. (b) Calculate the Mr of the chain. (c) The chain is part of a glycogen molecule with 2 branch points. State the type of glycosidic bond at each branch point and explain how branching helps animals.
items.answer: (a) 7 (b) 1,314 (c) 1,6 glycosidic bonds; many ends allow enzymes to hydrolyse glycogen rapidly to release glucose for respiration.

items.stem: A researcher in Cape Town extracts the main polysaccharide from cotton fibres and finds that it is cellulose. (a) Describe how two α-glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction. (b) Describe how cellulose could be hydrolysed to release glucose.
items.answer: (a) Condensation between the OH on C1 of one glucose and the OH on C4 of the other; water removed; 1,4 glycosidic bond formed. (b) Glycosidic bonds broken by adding water, catalysed by enzymes (amylase / glycogen phosphorylase, or cellulase for cellulose) or by boiling with acid.
items.markingKey: (a) C1 and C4 [1]; water removed [1]; 1,4 glycosidic bond [1] [3] (b) water added to glycosidic bonds [1]; enzyme / acid named [1] [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Cairo extracts the main polysaccharide from wheat endosperm and finds that it is starch. (a) Describe how two α-glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction. (b) Describe how starch could be hydrolysed to release glucose.
items.answer: (a) Condensation between the OH on C1 of one glucose and the OH on C4 of the other; water removed; 1,4 glycosidic bond formed. (b) Glycosidic bonds broken by adding water, catalysed by enzymes (amylase / glycogen phosphorylase, or cellulase for cellulose) or by boiling with acid.
items.markingKey: (a) C1 and C4 [1]; water removed [1]; 1,4 glycosidic bond [1] [3] (b) water added to glycosidic bonds [1]; enzyme / acid named [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "glycogen"?
options: A polysaccharide of β-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds forming straight chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.
A sugar made of two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, e.g. maltose, sucrose, lactose.
A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or ribose, with the general formula (CH₂O)n.
The highly branched storage polysaccharide of animals and fungi, made of α-glucose.
items.answer: The highly branched storage polysaccharide of animals and fungi, made of α-glucose.
items.markingKey: Glycogen: the highly branched storage polysaccharide of animals and fungi, made of α-glucose.

items.stem: A polysaccharide is made of α-glucose joined by 1,4 and 1,6 (branch about every 10 units) glycosidic bonds and is highly branched, compact. Which polysaccharide is it?
options: Cellulose
Glycogen
Amylose
Amylopectin
items.answer: Glycogen
items.markingKey: Glycogen: α-glucose, 1,4 and 1,6 (branch about every 10 units), highly branched, compact; energy store in animal liver and muscle; many ends for rapid hydrolysis to glucose.

items.stem: The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. What is the Mr of a chain of 20 glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds?
Compare the structures of amylose and glycogen, and relate one difference to their functions.
items.answer: Amylose: α-glucose, 1,4 only bonds, unbranched helix; compact energy store in plants; insoluble, no osmotic effect. Glycogen: α-glucose, 1,4 and 1,6 (branch about every 10 units) bonds, highly branched, compact; energy store in animal liver and muscle; many ends for rapid hydrolysis to glucose.
items.markingKey: monomer comparison [1]; bond type / branching [1]; shape [1]; difference linked to function [1] [4]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "saturated fatty acid"?
options: A lipid in which one fatty acid of a triglyceride is replaced by a phosphate-containing group, giving a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.
Repelled by water; non-polar, so does not mix with or dissolve in water.
A fatty acid with one or more C=C double bonds, which put kinks in the chain.
A fatty acid with no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
items.answer: A fatty acid with no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
items.markingKey: Saturated fatty acid: a fatty acid with no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.

items.stem: Explain why triglycerides are insoluble in water.
items.answer: Their fatty acid hydrocarbon tails are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; the ester bonds hide the polar groups.
items.markingKey: non-polar / hydrophobic tails [1]; no hydrogen bonds with water [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how phospholipids form a bilayer in cell membranes.
items.answer: The hydrophilic phosphate heads face the aqueous cytoplasm and tissue fluid, while the hydrophobic fatty acid tails face inwards away from water, forming two layers.
items.markingKey: heads face water [1]; tails inwards [1] [2]

items.stem: A triglyceride is formed from glycerol (Mr 92) and three fatty acids: myristic acid (Mr 228), myristic acid (Mr 228), stearic acid (Mr 284). (a) State the number of ester bonds and of water molecules released. (b) Calculate the Mr of the triglyceride (Mr of water = 18).
items.answer: (a) 3 ester bonds; 3 water molecules (b) 778

items.stem: A triglyceride is formed from glycerol (Mr 92) and three fatty acids: palmitic acid (Mr 256), stearic acid (Mr 284), stearic acid (Mr 284). (a) State the number of ester bonds and of water molecules released. (b) Calculate the Mr of the triglyceride (Mr of water = 18). (c) Predict whether this triglyceride is more likely to be a fat or an oil at room temperature, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 3 ester bonds; 3 water molecules (b) 862 (c) A fat (solid): saturated chains are straight and pack closely, so the melting point is high.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 and 3 [1] (b) 92 + 256 + 284 + 284 = 916 [1]; − 54 = 862 [1] (c) correct prediction [1]; kinks / packing explanation [1] [5]

items.stem: An Arctic fox living in a cold environment has a layer of blubber about 8 cm thick, made mainly of triglycerides. (a) Explain two ways in which the blubber helps the animal survive. (b) Describe how to test a sample of blubber for lipid.
items.answer: (a) Thermal insulation reduces heat loss; energy store for times when food is scarce; buoyancy. (b) Grind with ethanol, decant into water: white emulsion forms.
items.markingKey: (a) two functions explained [2] (b) Grind with ethanol [1]; decant into water: white emulsion forms [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why camels store fat in their humps rather than water.
items.answer: Respiration of fat releases a large amount of metabolic water as well as energy, and fat is a compact, high-energy store.
items.markingKey: metabolic water [1]; energy dense [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a triglyceride and of a phospholipid and explain how their structures are related to their roles in organisms.
items.answer: Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids by ester bonds (condensation), hydrophobic, energy store, insulation, metabolic water. Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate head, amphipathic, forms bilayers in membranes.
items.markingKey: triglyceride structure [2]; functions [2]; phospholipid structure [1]; bilayer explanation [1] [6]

items.stem: An Arctic fox living in a cold environment has a layer of blubber about 4 cm thick, made mainly of triglycerides. (a) Describe the structure of a triglyceride molecule. (b) Suggest why the triglycerides in the animal's feet contain more unsaturated fatty acids. (c) Describe how to test a sample of blubber for lipid.
items.answer: (a) One glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds formed in condensation reactions. (b) Unsaturated fats have lower melting points so they stay liquid / flexible at low temperatures. (c) Grind with ethanol, decant into water: white emulsion forms.
items.markingKey: (a) One glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds formed in condensation reactions [2] [2] (b) Unsaturated fats have lower melting points so they stay liquid / flexible at low temperatures [2] [2] (c) Grind with ethanol [1]; decant into water: white emulsion forms [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "secondary structure"?
options: The association of two or more polypeptide chains (and sometimes prosthetic groups) in a protein.
The regular coiling (α-helix) or folding (β-pleated sheet) of a polypeptide held by hydrogen bonds between –C=O and –NH groups.
The C–N bond formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of another.
The overall 3-D folding of a polypeptide held by hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions between R groups.
items.answer: The regular coiling (α-helix) or folding (β-pleated sheet) of a polypeptide held by hydrogen bonds between –C=O and –NH groups.
items.markingKey: Secondary structure: the regular coiling (α-helix) or folding (β-pleated sheet) of a polypeptide held by hydrogen bonds between –C=O and –NH groups.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of haemoglobin is related to its function.
items.answer: Globular and soluble so it is carried in red blood cells; four polypeptides each with a haem group containing Fe²⁺ that binds O₂, so each molecule carries 4 O₂; hydrophobic R groups inside, hydrophilic outside; quaternary structure allows cooperative binding.
items.markingKey: soluble / globular [1]; four haem groups / Fe²⁺ bind O₂ [1]; hydrophilic outside [1]; cooperative binding / shape change [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of collagen is related to its function.
items.answer: Three polypeptide chains wound into a triple helix with glycine every third residue allowing tight packing; hydrogen bonds between chains; molecules cross-linked covalently into staggered fibrils and fibres, giving high tensile strength in tendons, skin and bone.
items.markingKey: triple helix [1]; glycine / tight packing [1]; cross-links / fibrils [1]; tensile strength [1] [4]

items.stem: A collagen molecule is made of 3 polypeptide chains containing 1012 and 1012 and 1012 amino acids. (a) Calculate the number of peptide bonds. (b) Taking the mean Mr of an amino acid as 128 and of water as 18, estimate the Mr of the protein (ignore any prosthetic groups).

A single-chain hormone is made of 1 polypeptide chain containing 58 amino acids. (a) Calculate the number of peptide bonds. (b) Taking the mean Mr of an amino acid as 128 and of water as 18, estimate the Mr of the protein (ignore any prosthetic groups). (c) State the level of protein structure shown by a protein with more than one polypeptide chain, and name the bonds that may hold the chains together.
items.answer: (a) 57 (b) 6,398 (c) Quaternary structure; hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions.

items.stem: Insulin is made of 2 polypeptide chains containing 21 and 30 amino acids. (a) Calculate the number of peptide bonds. (b) Taking the mean Mr of an amino acid as 128 and of water as 18, estimate the Mr of the protein (ignore any prosthetic groups). (c) State the level of protein structure shown by a protein with more than one polypeptide chain, and name the bonds that may hold the chains together.
items.answer: (a) 49 (b) 5,646 (c) Quaternary structure; hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions.

items.stem: Keratin is a fibrous protein that forms hair and nails. A student in Dhaka researches how its structure relates to its function. (a) Suggest the effect on the function of keratin of heating it to 80 °C. (b) Describe how a peptide bond is formed.
items.answer: (a) Hydrogen and ionic bonds break, so the 3-D shape is lost (denatured); it can no longer carry out its function. (b) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next, removing water and forming –CO–NH–.
items.markingKey: (a) Hydrogen and ionic bonds break, so the 3-D shape is lost (denatured) [1]; it can no longer carry out its function [1] [2] (b) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next [1]; removing water and forming –CO–NH– [1] [2]

items.stem: Keratin is a fibrous protein that forms hair and nails. A student in Dubai researches how its structure relates to its function. (a) Describe what is meant by the primary, secondary and tertiary structure of a protein. (b) Describe how a peptide bond is formed.
items.answer: (a) Primary: amino acid sequence; secondary: α-helix / β-pleated sheet held by H-bonds between backbone groups; tertiary: 3-D folding held by bonds between R groups. (b) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next, removing water and forming –CO–NH–.
items.markingKey: (a) Primary: amino acid sequence [1]; secondary: α-helix / β-pleated sheet held by H-bonds between backbone groups [1]; tertiary: 3-D folding held by bonds between R groups [1] [3] (b) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next [1]; removing water and forming –CO–NH– [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a change in one amino acid can change the function of a protein.
items.answer: The primary structure determines how the chain folds; a different R group may form different bonds, changing the tertiary structure and so the shape of the active site or binding site.
items.markingKey: primary determines folding [1]; different R group bonds [1]; shape / function changes [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why high temperature denatures proteins but does not break peptide bonds.
items.answer: Heat increases kinetic energy, breaking weak hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the tertiary structure; strong covalent peptide bonds remain, so the primary structure is unchanged.
items.markingKey: hydrogen / ionic bonds broken [1]; tertiary shape lost [1]; peptide bonds covalent and stable [1] [3]

items.stem: Phenylalanine (Mr 165) and serine (Mr 105) join by a condensation reaction. (a) Name the bond formed and the groups that react. (b) Calculate the Mr of the dipeptide (Mr water = 18).
items.answer: (a) Peptide bond; carboxyl (–COOH) group of one amino acid and amine (–NH₂) group of the other (b) 252

items.stem: Haemoglobin is made of 4 polypeptide chains containing 141 and 141 and 146 and 146 amino acids. (a) Calculate the number of peptide bonds. (b) Taking the mean Mr of an amino acid as 128 and of water as 18, estimate the Mr of the protein (ignore any prosthetic groups). (c) State the level of protein structure shown by a protein with more than one polypeptide chain, and name the bonds that may hold the chains together.
items.answer: (a) 570 (b) 63,212 (c) Quaternary structure; hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "latent heat of vaporisation"?
options: A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom of one molecule and a slightly negative atom (such as oxygen) of another.
The attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding.
A liquid in which solutes dissolve; water dissolves polar and ionic substances.
The energy needed to change a liquid into a gas without a change in temperature (about 2.4 kJ g⁻¹ for water).
items.answer: The energy needed to change a liquid into a gas without a change in temperature (about 2.4 kJ g⁻¹ for water).
items.markingKey: Latent heat of vaporisation: the energy needed to change a liquid into a gas without a change in temperature (about 2.4 kJ g⁻¹ for water).

items.stem: Explain why water has a high specific heat capacity and why this is important to organisms.
items.answer: Hydrogen bonds restrict movement of molecules, so much energy is needed to raise temperature; body and habitat temperatures remain stable, so enzymes work efficiently.
items.markingKey: H-bonds absorb energy [1]; stable temperature [1]; enzymes / habitats [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why ice floats and why this is important for aquatic organisms.
items.answer: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold molecules further apart in a lattice, so ice is less dense than water; ice forms on the surface and insulates the water below, so it does not freeze and organisms survive.
items.markingKey: lattice / less dense [1]; insulates water below [1] [2]

items.stem: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.4 kJ g⁻¹. A marathon runner in Mexico City loses 1.5 dm³ (= 1500 g) of sweat, all of which evaporates. (a) Calculate the energy removed from the body.

The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.4 kJ g⁻¹. A marathon runner in Lima loses 1 dm³ (= 1000 g) of sweat, all of which evaporates. (a) Calculate the energy removed from the body. (b) The body has a mass of 55 kg and a mean specific heat capacity of 3.5 kJ kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Calculate the rise in body temperature that would have occurred if this energy had not been removed.

In winter, the air above Lake Baikal falls to −20 °C. The surface freezes, but the water at the bottom stays at about 4 °C, and fish survive. (a) Explain how the ice layer helps the fish survive. (b) Describe how hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
items.answer: (a) Ice insulates the water below, reducing heat loss, so water stays liquid; fish can still move and obtain oxygen. (b) Water is polar (δ⁻ O, δ⁺ H); δ⁺ H of one molecule attracts δ⁻ O of another.
items.markingKey: (a) Ice insulates the water below, reducing heat loss, so water stays liquid [1]; fish can still move and obtain oxygen [1] [2] (b) Water is polar (δ⁻ O, δ⁺ H) [1]; δ⁺ H of one molecule attracts δ⁻ O of another [1] [2]

items.stem: Which property of water explains this: columns of water can be pulled up xylem vessels in the transpiration stream?
options: Good solvent
Cohesion
High specific heat capacity
High surface tension
items.answer: Cohesion
items.markingKey: Cohesion: hydrogen bonds attract water molecules to one another.

items.stem: Explain how water acts as a solvent for sodium chloride.
items.answer: Water molecules are dipoles; δ⁻ oxygens surround Na⁺ and δ⁺ hydrogens surround Cl⁻, separating the ions.
items.markingKey: Water molecules are dipoles [1]; δ⁻ oxygens surround Na⁺ and δ⁺ hydrogens surround Cl⁻, separating the ions [1] [2]

items.stem: Which colour change shows a positive result in the test for lipid?
options: Blue → purple / lilac
Clear → white (milky) emulsion
Orange-brown → blue-black
Blue → colourless
items.answer: Clear → white (milky) emulsion
items.markingKey: Lipid: clear → white (milky) emulsion.

items.stem: Explain why Benedict's test is described as semi-quantitative.
items.answer: The colour of the precipitate depends on the concentration of reducing sugar, so it can be compared with standards to estimate concentration, but cannot give an exact value.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: The colour of the precipitate depends on the concentration of reducing sugar; so it can be compared with standards to estimate concentration; but cannot give an exact value (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Mohammed has a 10 % sucrose solution and distilled water. Copy and complete a table to show the volumes needed to make 20 cm³ of each of these concentrations: 1 %, 2 %, 7.5 %.
items.answer: 1 %: 2 cm³ stock + 18 cm³ water; 2 %: 4 cm³ stock + 16 cm³ water; 7.5 %: 15 cm³ stock + 5 cm³ water.
items.markingKey: V(stock) = C ÷ 10 × 20; one mark per correct row [3]

items.stem: Describe the tests you would use to identify reducing sugars, non-reducing sugars, starch, lipids and proteins, giving positive results.
items.answer: Reducing: Benedict's, heat, brick-red. Non-reducing: acid hydrolysis, neutralise, Benedict's. Starch: iodine, blue-black. Lipid: ethanol emulsion, white. Protein: biuret, purple.
items.markingKey: one mark per test with result [5]; control or semi-quantitative point [1] [6]

items.stem: Which monosaccharides make up maltose?
options: β-galactose and α-glucose
Fructose and galactose
Two β-glucose molecules
Two α-glucose molecules
items.answer: Two α-glucose molecules
items.markingKey: Maltose: two α-glucose molecules.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of cellulose is related to its function in plant cell walls.
items.answer: β-glucose with alternate units rotated 180° form straight chains; many hydrogen bonds link parallel chains into microfibrils, which are laid in layers giving high tensile strength so cells do not burst.
items.markingKey: β-glucose / alternate rotation [1]; straight chains [1]; hydrogen bonds / microfibrils [1]; tensile strength [1] [4]

items.stem: An unbranched chain of 10 α-glucose molecules is made by condensation. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. (a) State the number of glycosidic bonds. (b) Calculate the Mr of the chain.
Compare the structures of cellulose and amylopectin, and relate one difference to their functions.
items.answer: Cellulose: β-glucose, 1,4 with alternate glucose rotated 180° bonds, straight chains, hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils; strength of plant cell walls; high tensile strength. Amylopectin: α-glucose, 1,4 and 1,6 (branch about every 25 units) bonds, branched; energy store in plants; branches allow faster hydrolysis.
items.markingKey: monomer comparison [1]; bond type / branching [1]; shape [1]; difference linked to function [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the molecular structure of starch, glycogen and cellulose and explain how each structure is related to its function.
items.answer: Starch: amylose helix (α 1,4) + amylopectin (α 1,4, 1,6), compact insoluble store. Glycogen: α-glucose, highly branched (1,6 every ~10), rapid hydrolysis. Cellulose: β-glucose 1,4, alternate units inverted, straight chains, H-bonds, microfibrils, tensile strength.
items.markingKey: starch structure [2]; glycogen [1]; cellulose [2]; function links [2] [7]

items.stem: State three functions of triglycerides in organisms.
items.answer: Energy store; thermal insulation; buoyancy; protection of organs; source of metabolic water.
items.markingKey: any 3 from: Energy store; thermal insulation; buoyancy; protection of organs; source of metabolic water (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Explain why unsaturated fatty acids make membranes more fluid.
items.answer: Double bonds cause kinks in the tails so phospholipids cannot pack closely together.
items.markingKey: Double bonds cause kinks in the tails so phospholipids cannot pack closely together [2] [2]

items.stem: Respiration of lipid releases about 39 kJ g⁻¹ and of carbohydrate about 17 kJ g⁻¹. A seed of a sunflower needs to store 800 kJ of energy. (a) Calculate the mass of lipid and of carbohydrate needed. (b) Calculate the mass saved by storing lipid.
items.answer: (a) lipid 20.5 g; carbohydrate 47.1 g (b) 26.5 g

items.stem: Samuel says: "Peptide bonds are broken when a protein is denatured." Explain whether Samuel is correct.
items.answer: Denaturation breaks hydrogen, ionic and sometimes disulfide bonds; peptide bonds remain intact.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Denaturation breaks hydrogen, ionic and sometimes disulfide bonds; peptide bonds remain intact. [2]

items.stem: Sofia says: "Peptide bonds are broken when a protein is denatured." Explain whether Sofia is correct.
items.answer: Denaturation breaks hydrogen, ionic and sometimes disulfide bonds; peptide bonds remain intact.

items.stem: A single-chain hormone is made of 1 polypeptide chain containing 28 amino acids. (a) Calculate the number of peptide bonds. (b) Taking the mean Mr of an amino acid as 128 and of water as 18, estimate the Mr of the protein (ignore any prosthetic groups).
Compare the structures of haemoglobin and collagen and explain how each is related to its function.
items.answer: Haemoglobin: globular, 4 polypeptides (2α 2β), haem with Fe²⁺, soluble, hydrophilic outside, binds 4 O₂. Collagen: fibrous, 3 polypeptides in triple helix, glycine every third, H-bonds, cross-links into fibrils and fibres, insoluble, tensile strength.

items.stem: Haemoglobin is a globular protein that transports oxygen in red blood cells. A student in Hanoi researches how its structure relates to its function. (a) Describe what is meant by the primary, secondary and tertiary structure of a protein. (b) Explain why haemoglobin is described as globular.
items.answer: (a) Primary: amino acid sequence; secondary: α-helix / β-pleated sheet held by H-bonds between backbone groups; tertiary: 3-D folding held by bonds between R groups. (b) Globular: compact, spherical, soluble, hydrophilic R groups outside.

items.stem: A student in Hanoi states: "Ice sinks because it is solid." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water and floats, because hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open lattice.

items.stem: Explain how the good solvent of water is important to living organisms.
items.answer: Polar and ionic substances dissolve, so it is a medium for reactions and transport in blood, xylem and phloem; water molecules are dipoles that cluster around ions and polar molecules.
items.markingKey: importance [1]; explained by hydrogen bonding / dipoles [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how (i) the high specific heat capacity and (ii) the high surface tension of water are important to living organisms, referring to hydrogen bonding.
items.answer: (i) Water temperature changes slowly, so aquatic habitats and the internal temperature of organisms stay stable; many hydrogen bonds must be broken to increase molecular motion. (ii) Small organisms such as pond skaters can walk on the surface; cohesion between molecules at the surface.
items.markingKey: (i) importance [1]; explanation [1] (ii) importance [1]; explanation [1] [4]

items.stem: Grace carried out a semi-quantitative Benedict's test. (a) Estimate the concentration of reducing sugar in the sample. (b) Suggest how the method could be improved to give a more precise value.
items.answer: (a) Between 0.25% and 0.5% (b) Use a colorimeter to measure absorbance / transmission (after filtering the precipitate) and plot a calibration curve; or use more standards with smaller intervals.

items.stem: A food-science student in Hanoi is asked to find out which biological molecules are present in a powdered infant formula. (a) Describe how the student would test for protein and state the positive result. (b) Suggest a suitable negative control for these tests. (c) Suggest how the student could compare the concentration of reducing sugar in two brands.
items.answer: (a) Add biuret reagent (or NaOH then dilute CuSO₄) to a solution of the food; blue → purple. (b) Repeat each test with distilled water instead of the food sample to show the reagents alone do not give a positive result. (c) Use the same volume of each with the same volume of Benedict's, same temperature and time, then compare colour with standards or use a colorimeter / mass of precipitate.

items.stem: What is the difference between α-glucose and β-glucose?
options: β-glucose is a pentose
The position of the –OH on carbon 6
The number of carbon atoms
The position of the –H and –OH groups on carbon atom 1
items.answer: The position of the –H and –OH groups on carbon atom 1
items.markingKey: In α-glucose the OH on C1 is below the ring; in β-glucose it is above.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the structure of starch makes it suitable as a storage molecule. (b) Explain why glycogen is more suitable than starch as an energy store in animals.
items.answer: (a) Insoluble, so no osmotic effect and does not diffuse out of cells; compact (helical amylose); branched amylopectin gives many ends for rapid hydrolysis; made of α-glucose, easily hydrolysed to glucose for respiration. (b) Glycogen is more highly branched, so has more ends for enzymes to act on, allowing glucose to be released more rapidly for the higher metabolic rate of animals.

items.stem: An unbranched chain of 1000 α-glucose molecules is made by condensation. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. (a) State the number of glycosidic bonds. (b) Calculate the Mr of the chain.
Compare the structures of glycogen and amylose, and relate one difference to their functions.
items.answer: Glycogen: α-glucose, 1,4 and 1,6 (branch about every 10 units) bonds, highly branched, compact; energy store in animal liver and muscle; many ends for rapid hydrolysis to glucose. Amylose: α-glucose, 1,4 only bonds, unbranched helix; compact energy store in plants; insoluble, no osmotic effect.

items.stem: A researcher in Doha extracts the main polysaccharide from wheat endosperm and finds that it is starch. (a) Describe how two α-glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction. (b) Describe how starch could be hydrolysed to release glucose. (c) Describe how to test the extract for starch and state the expected result.
items.answer: (a) Condensation between the OH on C1 of one glucose and the OH on C4 of the other; water removed; 1,4 glycosidic bond formed. (b) Glycosidic bonds broken by adding water, catalysed by enzymes (amylase / glycogen phosphorylase, or cellulase for cellulose) or by boiling with acid. (c) Add iodine in potassium iodide solution: orange-brown to blue-black.

items.stem: Describe how a phospholipid differs from a triglyceride.
